title: When Python Must Decide What a Class Means
key_insight: Python has separate rulebooks for choosing between inherited methods, building class blueprints, and letting threads take turns with pure Python work.
body:
## Who Gets the Next Turn?

A child class has two parents, and both offer the same method. Python writes one fair lookup route called the method resolution order; its C3 rule keeps earlier family promises from being silently reversed.

Before any object exists, something must build the class blueprint itself. That class-builder is called a metaclass; frameworks can use it to check or register a class as soon as the blueprint is made.

Now picture one key for the pure-Python workroom. CPython's Global Interpreter Lock lets one thread hold that key at a time, though waiting jobs and fast outside libraries can release it.
common_mistakes: Thinking the parent-call helper always names one fixed parent — it continues along Python’s chosen lookup route.
Using a class-building rulebook for a check that could happen more simply when an ordinary object is created.
Saying the interpreter lock stops every kind of parallel work — waiting tasks and many fast numerical libraries can release it.
Combining several parent classes when their methods expect different inputs or refuse to pass control onward.
mini_exercise: Create three small parent classes that each print its name and pass control onward. Swap the first two parents, print Python’s lookup route, and predict the new print order.
real_world_usage: Frameworks can inspect a class when its blueprint is created, while numerical libraries send heavy calculations to fast compiled code that can work outside Python’s one-at-a-time lock.
explain_back_prompt: Using the family-route, blueprint-builder, and workroom-key stories, explain the job of the method lookup order, its consistency rule, a metaclass, and the interpreter lock.
